algorithm: Lloyd's k-means: assign, recompute, repeat until convergence
complexity: O(n*k*i) for n points, k clusters, i iterations
data_flow_ascii:
--seed -> generate_points (k Gaussian blobs)
points -> kmeans: assign -> recompute -> ...
(centroids, labels) -> inertia + cluster table
description_sentence: Runs Lloyd's k-means on seeded 2-D synthetic points and prints final centroids, cluster sizes, and inertia.
failure_note: An empty cluster keeps its previous centroid instead of producing NaNs; iteration stops early when centroids stop moving.

functions.desc: Generate 2-D points around k random topic centers.
functions.name: generate_points

functions.desc: Assign each point to its nearest centroid; return label list.
functions.name: assign

functions.desc: Recompute centroids as cluster means; keep old center if empty.
functions.name: recompute

functions.desc: Sum of squared distances of points to their assigned centroid.
functions.name: inertia

functions.desc: Parse args, cluster, and print centroids and inertia.
functions.name: main

label: K-means clustering
output_shape: A cluster table (id, centroid x/y, size) and the final inertia value.
pitch_sentence: A {topic} k-means implementation in pure Python running Lloyd's algorithm on seeded blobs, printing centroids, sizes, and inertia.

qa.a: Random data points sampled with the seed, which is the standard k-means++-free initialization; results stay deterministic per seed.
Yes; lower inertia means tighter clusters, and the demo prints it after the final assignment.
Use --k, --n, and --iterations to change the cluster count, point count, and iteration cap.
qa.q: Can the demo shape be changed?

resume_bullet_template: Built a {topic} k-means clustering tool in pure Python implementing Lloyd's algorithm (nearest-centroid assignment, mean recomputation) on seeded synthetic data; demo prints centroids, cluster sizes, and inertia.
scaling_note: Pure-Python distance loops are O(n*k) per iteration, so large datasets would need numpy vectorization.
storage_note: In-memory only: points, centroids, and labels exist for the run and are not persisted.
tradeoff_note: Hand-written Lloyd's is transparent and dependency-free, but lacks k-means++ seeding and mini-batch variants for big data.
